Volume 13 · Chapter 04

General equilibrium and existence

Graduate Author-reviewed · Prerequisites: v13-c03

By the endExplain and apply equilibrium existence arguments and their assumptions.

Volume 13 · Chapter 4

General equilibrium and existence

A household can choose optimally at quoted prices while its proposed purchases cannot be supplied. A firm can maximize profit while no buyer can finance its output. General equilibrium asks whether one price system can make all those choices compatible, including the ownership income that pays for demand. Existence is a theorem about that compatibility. It does not identify which equilibrium will occur or how a market reaches it.

Capability. Reconcile exchange and production accounts; prove the finite-dimensional chain from Sperner’s lemma to Brouwer’s and Kakutani’s fixed-point theorems; apply it to a precisely specified private-ownership economy; and diagnose failures of existence, uniqueness and iterative convergence. Six worked cases and twelve solved exercises connect the proof to quantities and counterexamples.

Prerequisites. Preference representation and choice supplies continuous utility and convex preferences; Consumer and producer duality supplies budget and profit problems. Uncertainty and information distinguishes a deterministic bundle from a lottery over bundles. We use finite-dimensional compactness, continuity and convexity from convex optimization and real analysis. No fixed-point theorem or Nash existence theorem is assumed in the proof chain below.

1. Choices, ownership and the accounts that must add up

There are finitely many goods ℓ=1,…,L, households i=1,…,I and firms j=1,…,J, with I≥1 and possibly J=0. Household i consumes xi∈ℝ+L and owns endowment ωi. A firm’s net supply yj has negative input components and positive output components. Its technology is Yj. All quantities refer to the same declared commodity, date and location; the static model has no unrecorded borrowing or transfers. Let θij≥0 be household i’s share of firm j, with Σiθij=1 for each firm.

At a nonzero price vector p≥0, define profit, household income and aggregate excess demand by

πj(p)=maxy∈Yj p·y,   mi(p)=p·ωi+Σjθijπj(p),
z(x,y)=Σixi−Σiωi−Σjyj.

A competitive equilibrium consists of prices and choices such that every firm maximizes profit, every household chooses a most-preferred bundle among x≥0 with p·x≤mi(p), and z=0. The maximum notation presumes existence, which must be established under the relevant assumptions. At prices with multiple optima, demand and supply are sets, called correspondences, rather than single-valued functions.

Walras accounting. At actual profit-maximizing supplies p·yj=πj(p). Summing the household budget inequalities and using the ownership sums gives

p·Σixi≤p·Σiωi+Σjπj(p)=p·(Σiωi+Σjyj),
so p·z≤0.

If all budgets are exhausted, equality gives Walras law, p·z=0. This is a value identity, not the vector equality z=0. With positive prices, clearing all but one market and Walras law clears the last; a zero price prevents that inference for its commodity. Omitting distributed profits or counting input purchases twice breaks the accounting rather than refuting the identity.

Multiplying every price by t>0 multiplies profits and incomes by t and leaves all affordable sets and maximizers unchanged. Thus normalize prices to the simplex Δ={p≥0:Σℓpℓ=1}. In two-good calculations with p₂>0 it is often easier to set p₂=1; that is the same relative-price information in a different normalization. An existence proof must still handle, or exclude, the boundary of Δ.

Worked case 1: exchange, income feedback and a new endowment

Two households have endowments ((4,1),(1,4)) and Cobb–Douglas first-good shares (2/3,1/3): u₁=x₁2/3x₂1/3 and u₂=x₁1/3x₂2/3. Write p=(r,1), r>0. At wealth m>0 and share 0<α<1, a bundle with both goods positive is feasible and has positive utility; an axis bundle has zero utility. An optimum is therefore interior and spends m. Maximizing α log x₁+(1−α)log x₂ on the budget gives x₁=αm/r and x₂=(1−α)m. The logarithm is strictly concave on the positive orthant, so its stationary budget solution is the unique global optimum.

Here m₁=4r+1 and m₂=r+4. Total first-good demand is (2/3)(4r+1)/r+(1/3)(r+4)/r=3+2/r. Supply is 5, so the unique positive relative price is 1. Incomes are (5,5), and household allocations are ((10/3,5/3),(5/3,10/3)). Each bundle costs its owner’s income; aggregate consumption is (5,5). The second market clears directly and also follows from Walras law.

Now give household 1 one more unit of the second good, making its endowment (4,2). Wealth changes with the equilibrium price: m₁=4r+2, m₂=r+4. First-good demand is 3+8/(3r), so r=4/3. Incomes become (22/3,16/3), and allocations become ((11/3,22/9),(4/3,32/9)), summing to (5,6). Holding incomes at their old values would miss the endowment-price feedback.

No zero-price equilibrium was omitted. If one good is free, the strictly positive endowment supplies positive income in the other good. Buy a positive amount of that priced good and increase the free good without bound; utility has no finite maximum. The direct argument therefore establishes uniqueness for each of these two economies. Cobb–Douglas preferences are weakly monotone on the whole orthant, but an increase along an axis can leave utility zero. These cases are proved directly; they are not applications of the stronger global strict-coordinate-monotonicity theorem in Section 5.

Worked case 2: production profits belong in somebody’s budget

The goods are input/leisure and consumption output. Each household owns (2,1/2) and has utility √(x₁x₂). Firm ownership shares are (1/4,3/4). The firm has compact generator K={ (−n,q):0≤n≤4, 0≤q≤2√n }, followed by free disposal: Y=K−ℝ+2. K is compact and contains zero. It is convex because the hypograph of the concave function 2√n is convex; mapping n to −n preserves convexity. Its capacity is 4.

Normalize the output price to 1 and write the input price as w>0. Profit maximization sets q=2√n. With t=√n∈[0,2], profit is 2t−wt². Completing the square gives an unconstrained maximizer t=1/w. Thus for w>1/2, input n=1/w², output q=2/w and profit π=1/w. For 0<w≤1/2, capacity binds: (n,q)=(4,4) and π=4−4w. In this capacity branch the available leisure is zero, whereas positive wealth makes both households demand positive leisure. It cannot be an equilibrium.

In the interior branch total income is 4w+1+1/w. Half is spent on leisure, so its market equation is (4w+1+1/w)/(2w)=4−1/w². Equivalently 4w²−w−3=0, with roots (1,−3/4). The sole admissible wage is 1. Net supply is (−1,2), profit 1, and individual incomes are 2w+1/2+θiπ, hence (11/4,13/4). Demands are ((11/8,11/8),(13/8,13/8)). Their sum (3,3) equals the aggregate endowment (4,1) plus net supply (−1,2). This accounts for leisure consumed, input used, output produced and distributed profit exactly once.

Give each household half the firm. Total income and the common expenditure shares stay the same, so wage and production remain unchanged, while incomes become (3,3) and allocations ((3/2,3/2),(3/2,3/2)). Ownership affects distribution here. Its lack of a price effect relies on the identical expenditure shares; it is not a general ownership-irrelevance theorem. If profits are instead omitted, aggregate demand at w=1 is (5/2,5/2) against resources (3,3), giving p·z=−1. A unit of value has disappeared from household budgets.

At zero wage, positive income in output permits unbounded desired free leisure. At zero output price and a positive wage, households can buy positive leisure and increase free output without limit. Those prices give no household optimum. As in case 1, the boundary behavior of √(x₁x₂) is handled directly rather than attributed to the later stronger preference assumption.

2. A combinatorial route to a fixed point

Existence arguments need not specify an adjustment process. The proof begins with a finite counting result and then passes to a limit. For integer d≥0 let Δd={x∈ℝd+1:xi≥0, Σi=0dxi=1}, the d-dimensional simplex with vertices e₀,…,ed. A face is the convex hull of a subset of the vertices. A compatible triangulation is a finite subdivision into d-simplices whose union is Δd, whose intersections are common faces, and whose restrictions to original faces are triangulations there. The mesh is the largest diameter of a small simplex.

Why arbitrarily fine compatible triangulations exist. Let T have vertices v₁,…,vd+1. For each ordering i₁,…,id+1, form the chain Fk={vi₁,…,vik} and the simplex with vertices b(Fk), their barycentres. To see coverage, express x=Σλivi, sort λi₁≥⋯≥λid+1≥λid+2=0, and set

μk=k(λik−λik+1),   k=1,…,d+1.
μk≥0,   Σkμk=Σiλi=1,   x=Σkμkb(Fk).

The last identity follows because the coefficient of vir on its right is Σk≥rμk/k=λir. The chain’s barycentres are affinely independent: their coordinates in the ordered vertices have triangular columns with nonzero diagonal. Ties among adjacent λ’s set the corresponding μ’s to zero. The nonzero μ’s identify exactly the vertex sets above each strict coordinate drop. Thus two ordering regions meet in the face generated by their common surviving barycentres. If x lies on an original face, all outside λ’s are zero and only barycentres of that face survive. Subdividing adjacent simplices consequently agrees on their shared face. This proves the required coverage and compatibility, not just a picture in dimension two.

For nested nonempty faces F⊂G, b(G)=(|F|/|G|)b(F)+(1−|F|/|G|)b(G∖F). Hence

‖b(G)−b(F)‖≤(1−|F|/|G|) diam(T)≤[d/(d+1)] diam(T).

Every pair of vertices in a new simplex comes from nested faces. A convex hull has diameter no greater than the largest distance between its vertices, so each barycentric subdivision contracts mesh by at most d/(d+1) for d≥1. Repetition gives mesh tending to zero. For d=0 the simplex is a single point.

Sperner’s lemma. Label each triangulation vertex by one index in {0,…,d}, requiring that coordinate vi=0 forbids label i. Then the number of d-simplices carrying all d+1 labels is odd, and in particular at least one exists.

Proof by dimension and parity. For d=0 there is one vertex and its sole permitted label is 0. For d≥1, mark each (d−1)-facet whose vertices carry all labels 0,…,d−1. Count incidences between marked facets and d-simplices. A fully labeled d-simplex contributes one marked facet, obtained by deleting the vertex labeled d. A simplex using exactly labels 0,…,d−1, with one of them repeated, contributes two. All other simplices contribute zero. The incidence total modulo two is therefore the number of fully labeled d-simplices modulo two.

An interior facet has exactly two incident d-simplices and a boundary facet has one. To justify the incidence fact, take a point in the relative interior of the facet and a sufficiently small ball avoiding every other lower-dimensional face. The facet divides the ball into two sides. Coverage supplies a cell on each available side, while disjoint cell interiors permit at most one on each side; on the outside boundary only one side is available. Thus interior contributions are even. A marked boundary facet cannot lie on an original face opposite any i<d, because that face forbids label i. It must lie on the face opposite d. The restricted triangulation of that face satisfies the (d−1)-dimensional labeling rule, and by induction its number of marked facets is odd. The incidence total, and hence the number of fully labeled d-cells, is odd. This completes the induction.

The inspected Mathew note, sections 1–2 illustrates the two-dimensional parity and limiting ideas. The arbitrary-dimensional subdivision, mesh bound and induction needed here have been proved explicitly above. No claim about the note’s later valuation material is needed.

Worked case 3: a finite labeling certificate

On Δ² take f(x₀,x₁,x₂)=(x₁,x₂,x₀). At a nonfixed vertex label by the smallest i with vi>fi(v). Use the corners and edge midpoints in the order ((1,0,0),(0,1,0),(0,0,1),(1/2,1/2,0),(1/2,0,1/2),(0,1/2,1/2)). Number them 0,…,5. The four small cells are ((0,3,4),(1,3,5),(2,4,5),(3,4,5)).

Vertexv−f(v)Label
e₀(1,0,−1)0
e₁(−1,1,0)1
e₂(0,−1,1)2
m₀₁(0,1/2,−1/2)1
m₀₂(1/2,−1/2,0)0
m₁₂(−1/2,0,1/2)2

The label vector is (0,1,2,1,0,2). Only the central cell (3,4,5) is fully labeled. The numbers of marked {0,1} edges incident to the four cells are (2,0,0,1). Their total is odd: an interior marked edge contributes twice and a boundary marked edge once. The central centroid is (1/3,1/3,1/3); direct substitution shows it is the fixed point of this particular linear cycle. Generally a fully labeled cell is a finite certificate used in a limiting argument, not a claim that its centroid is an exact fixed point.

3. Brouwer’s theorem, including the compact-convex extension

Theorem. Every continuous f:Δd→Δd has a fixed point. For d=0 this is immediate. For d≥1 take the sequence of compatible triangulations just constructed. If a vertex v ever satisfies f(v)=v, the proof is finished. Otherwise Σi[vi−fi(v)]=0 and not all terms vanish, so at least one term is strictly positive. Label v by one such coordinate, for definiteness the smallest. A zero coordinate cannot receive its own label, since fi(v)≥0.

Sperner gives a full cell at each subdivision level n, with a vertex vn,i labeled i for every i. Compactness gives a subsequence of vn,0 converging to x. Since the mesh tends to zero, every vn,i along this same subsequence converges to x. The labeling inequalities and continuity give xi≥fi(x) for every i. Both coordinate sums equal 1, so every inequality is equality: f(x)=x. The chosen cells need not be nested. Compact subsequences and vanishing diameters are sufficient.

Projection lemma. If K⊂ℝn is nonempty compact and convex, every z∈ℝn has a unique nearest point PK(z). Existence follows by minimizing the continuous squared distance on compact K. If distinct a,b were both minimizers, their midpoint would be feasible and

‖z−(a+b)/2‖²=[‖z−a‖²+‖z−b‖²]/2−‖a−b‖²/4

would be strictly smaller. Write a=PK(z). For y∈K, the segment a+t(y−a) is feasible for 0≤t≤1. The right derivative at t=0 of its squared distance from z is nonnegative, giving (z−a)·(y−a)≤0. For b=PK(z′), apply this inequality with y=b and the analogous inequality for z′ with y=a. Adding and rearranging yields

‖a−b‖²≤(z−z′)·(a−b)≤‖z−z′‖‖a−b‖.

Thus ‖PK(z)−PK(z′)‖≤‖z−z′‖, including a=b. Projection is continuous; uniqueness and continuity have not been presumed.

To extend Brouwer, choose a>0 so K⊂[−a,a]n. For n≥1 the simplex with vertices v₀=−a1 and vi=v₀+2na ei, i=1,…,n, contains that cube: every cube point has nonnegative coordinates xi+a whose sum is at most 2na. A continuous map f:K→K extends to the simplex by g(z)=f(PK(z)). Its values lie in K and hence in the simplex. The simplex theorem, transported by affine coordinates, gives z=g(z). Since g(z)∈K, z∈K and PK(z)=z, so f(z)=z. For n=0 there is one point. We have proved Brouwer on every nonempty compact convex finite-dimensional set, even one with empty ambient interior.

4. From a continuous function to a correspondence

A correspondence F:K⇒K assigns a subset F(x) of K to each x. Its graph is {(x,y):y∈F(x)}. It is upper hemicontinuous at x if, for every open set O containing F(x), all values F(z) for z sufficiently close to x are contained in O. This prevents new distant choices from appearing near x. It does not require any arbitrarily chosen single-valued selection to be continuous.

Graph qualification. With compact range K and closed values, closed graph is equivalent to upper hemicontinuity. If a closed graph failed upper hemicontinuity, some open O⊃F(x) would admit xn→x and yn∈F(xn)∖O. Compactness supplies ynk→y; the complement of O is closed, so y∉O, whereas the closed graph gives y∈F(x), a contradiction. Conversely, if xn→x and yn→y with yn∈F(xn) but y∉F(x), compact closed F(x) has positive distance from y. An open neighborhood of F(x) separated from a small ball around y contradicts upper hemicontinuity for sufficiently large n. The compact-range hypothesis in the first direction cannot silently be dropped.

Kakutani’s theorem. If K is a nonempty compact convex subset of a finite-dimensional Euclidean space, F has a closed graph and every F(x) is nonempty, compact and convex, then some x satisfies x∈F(x).

Proof. For ε>0 compactness gives finitely many points x₁,…,xN∈K such that every x∈K is within ε/2 of at least one xj. Choose yj∈F(xj). Define continuous tent weights

wj(x)=max{0,ε−‖x−xj‖},   aj(x)=wj(x)/Σkwk(x),
gε(x)=Σjaj(x)yj.

The denominator is positive by the covering property. Convexity of K makes gε a continuous K-valued function, so the Brouwer theorem just proved gives xε=gε(xε). No continuity of the selections yj as a function of their sites was asserted.

Let εn↓0 and take a convergent subsequence xεn→x. Every active site, meaning one with positive weight at xεn, lies within εn of that point. Thus all active sites approach x uniformly. Given δ>0, upper hemicontinuity says every active selected value yj eventually lies within distance δ of F(x). Choose a nearest bj∈F(x) for each such yj. Convexity puts b=Σajbj in F(x), and

dist(xεn,F(x))≤‖Σjaj(yj−bj)‖≤Σjaj‖yj−bj‖<δ.

Since δ is arbitrary and F(x) is closed, the limit x belongs to F(x). This proves the theorem. Finiteness of the nets constructs continuous approximations; it is the limiting argument that proves existence.

Worked case 4: four hypotheses that cannot be erased

On K=[0,1], set F(x)={1} for x<1/2, F(1/2)={0,1}, and F(x)={0} for x>1/2. Its graph is the union of the two closed segments [0,1/2]×{1} and [1/2,1]×{0}, so it is closed. All values are nonempty compact, but the middle value is not convex. Below 1/2 the image 1 differs from x; above it the image 0 differs from x; at the midpoint neither image equals x. There is no fixed point. Replacing the middle value by [0,1] repairs convexity and gives the unique fixed point 1/2.

If instead F(1/2)={0}, every value is a convex singleton, but closed graph fails: xn=1/2−1/n for n≥3 has yn=1, and the limit pair (1/2,1) is absent. This variant has no fixed point either. On the disconnected domain K={0,1}, the swapping map 0↦1, 1↦0 is continuous in the relative topology and has no fixed point; the domain is not convex. Finally, on the noncompact domain [0,1), f(x)=(1+x)/2 is a continuous self-map. Its only algebraic fixed-point candidate is 1, which is excluded. None of these claims depends on a failed numerical search.

5. A complete sufficient production-existence theorem

The theorem will use a special production class whose feasible resource bounds can actually be proved. It is not a claim that all unbounded production economies satisfy the same conditions. Assume the following throughout this section.

  • Each household’s preferences on ℝ+L admit a continuous utility representation ui, have convex upper contour sets, and are strictly coordinate-monotone: y≥x with y≠x implies y≻ix. The representation theorem of Chapter 1 supplies the continuous representation under its stated continuous-order assumptions on the orthant; one may equivalently take the ui as primitives here.
  • Every household has ωi≫0 individually. This is stronger than positivity of aggregate resources. Ownership shares are nonnegative and sum to one for each firm.
  • Every firm has Yj=Kj−ℝ+L, where Kj is a nonempty compact convex set containing zero. This is a compact-generator technology with free disposal. There need not be any firms.

Theorem. Under these assumptions a competitive equilibrium exists with strictly positive prices, global household optimization on the original unbounded consumption orthant, profit maximization on the full technologies Yj, and exact market clearing.

The proof has four tasks: construct a compact product domain; prove the optimizer correspondences satisfy Kakutani’s hypotheses; derive feasible clearing and positive prices from its fixed point; and remove the artificial household caps. A fixed point of arbitrary truncated demands would not by itself finish the economic argument.

5.1 Profits, positive incomes and a legitimate resource cap

For p≥0 and any y=k−d∈Yj, d≥0, p·y≤p·k. Therefore the full technology’s maximum profit equals the support of Kj:

πj(p)=maxk∈Kjp·k,   Sj(p)=argmaxk∈Kjp·k.

The maximum exists by compactness; πj≥0 because zero is available. Write Rj=maxk∈Kj‖k‖. Comparing each support value with the other price gives |πj(p)−πj(q)|≤Rj‖p−q‖. Profits and incomes are continuous. On Δ,

mi(p)=p·ωi+Σjθijπj(p)≥minℓωiℓ>0.

We use Sj to choose a compact representative of profit-maximizing supply. At zero prices the full Yj may have an unbounded set of equally profitable disposal choices. Substituting that set into a purported compact correspondence would be an error; the representative still maximizes over the entire technology.

Define Aℓ=Σiωiℓ+Σjmaxk∈Kjkℓ. Each Aℓ is finite and positive. Choose one M>maxℓAℓ and let C=[0,M]L. Any feasible allocation using representatives yj∈Kj satisfies Σixiℓ≤Aℓ<M. This bound comes from actual endowments and technologies, not from the preferences or a guessed numerical price.

5.2 Derive the correspondence properties

The capped budget and demand correspondences are

BiM(p)={x∈C:p·x≤mi(p)},   DiM(p)=argmaxx∈BiM(p)ui(x).

BiM(p) is nonempty because it contains zero, and it is compact and convex. Its graph is closed: limits preserve C and the budget inequality, using continuous income. We also need to approximate any feasible choice at a limit price by choices feasible at nearby prices. If pn→p and x∈BiM(p), put tn=min{1,mi(pn)/(pn·x)} when the denominator is positive, and tn=1 otherwise. Then tnx is feasible and remains in C. If p·x<mi(p), feasibility holds with tn=1 eventually. If p·x=mi(p), the common value is strictly positive, so the ratio tends to one. In both cases tnx→x. Positive individual income is doing real work here.

Continuous ui attains a maximum on every compact budget, so DiM is nonempty and compact-valued. Its values are convex: if x and x′ both attain the maximal utility, convex upper contours make their mixture attain at least that utility, and convex budget feasibility prevents it from exceeding the maximum. To prove its graph closed, let pn→p, xn→x, and xn∈DiM(pn). Closed budget feasibility gives x∈BiM(p). For any z∈BiM(p), the approximation above gives zn∈BiM(pn) with zn→z. Optimality and continuity give ui(x)=lim ui(xn)≥lim ui(zn)=ui(z). Thus x is optimal. The proof supplies the optimizer-limit argument instead of citing an unchecked maximum theorem.

Sj(p) is nonempty compact and convex because it maximizes a linear function on compact convex Kj. Its graph is closed: pn·yn≥pn·k for every k∈Kj passes to the limit, with y∈Kj by closedness. Finally define the price-auction correspondence

A(z)=argmaxq∈Δq·z.

It selects normalized prices placing weight on the largest excess-demand coordinates. It is nonempty compact and convex. Its graph is closed because the maximizing inequality qn·zn≥r·zn, for every fixed r∈Δ, passes to the limit. No price-adjustment dynamics are specified by this construction.

5.3 Apply Kakutani, then prove that the fixed point clears

Use the nonempty compact convex product domain Z=Δ×CI×∏jKj, omitting the final factors when there are no firms. Define

T(p,x,y)=A(z(x,y))×∏iDiM(p)×∏jSj(p).

Every value is nonempty compact and convex. Closed graph follows component by component from the preceding results and continuity of z(x,y). Kakutani supplies a fixed point (p,x,y). Since demands satisfy their budgets and firm representatives earn the distributed profits, ownership accounting yields p·z≤0. Since p∈A(z), q·z≤p·z≤0 for every q∈Δ. In particular choose q=eℓ to get zℓ≤0 for each good. Thus the allocation is feasible with possible slack resources.

Feasibility now yields Σixiℓ≤Σiωiℓ+Σjyjℓ≤Aℓ<M. Every household consumption coordinate is strictly below its cap. If some pℓ=0, any capped maximizer would have xiℓ=M: otherwise increasing that free coordinate within C would strictly improve utility without changing cost. This contradicts the feasible resource bound. Therefore p≫0.

Each household also exhausts its budget. If it had slack, a sufficiently small increase in one coordinate would fit both the remaining budget and the strictly positive distance to the cap, and strict monotonicity would improve utility. Hence p·z=0. Since p≫0 and z≤0 componentwise, every component of z is zero. Notice the order: feasibility puts choices below the cap before budget exhaustion is inferred. Strict monotonicity does not imply nonsatiation at the maximal corner of an artificially bounded box.

5.4 Remove the household caps without assuming strict convexity

It remains to show each xi is optimal on the original, uncapped budget. Suppose an affordable x′≥0 satisfies x′≻ixi. It cannot be zero, since strict monotonicity makes zero no better than any nonnegative bundle. Continuity lets us choose t<1 sufficiently close to one that tx′≻ixi. Positive prices and income give p·tx′<mi(p). For a sufficiently small λ>0 the mixture b=(1−λ)xi+λtx′ stays in C, because every coordinate of xi is strictly below M. The mixture is strictly cheaper than mi(p) and is weakly preferred to xi by convex upper contours.

Ordinary convex preferences do not by themselves say that this mixture is strictly preferred. Instead use its cost slack and its position strictly below the cap: add a sufficiently small positive amount of one commodity to b, remaining in C and in the budget. Strict coordinate monotonicity makes the new bundle strictly preferred to b, hence strictly preferred to xi. This contradicts capped optimality. No preferred uncapped affordable bundle exists. Firm representatives already maximize over the full Yj, so the constructed point is an equilibrium of the original economy. This completes the theorem, including pure exchange.

Where each assumption enters. Compact generators bound supports and resources; convex generators and convex preferences give convex-valued optima; continuity and closed feasible sets support optimizer limits; positive individual endowments keep every budget perturbable even on the price boundary; strict monotonicity rules out free goods, establishes exhaustion below the cap, and completes cap removal. These are sufficient conditions. The theorem does not state that their failure always prevents equilibrium, or that every technology can be replaced by this compact class without changing the economy.

Tamuz’s notes, inspected pages 4–7 and 13–17, provide context for preferences, private ownership and price correspondences. Our compact-generator theorem and complete fixed-point proof state the precise scope used here. In particular, we do not adopt a general conical enlargement of technology, infer strict mixture improvements from convexity alone, or identify closed graph with upper hemicontinuity without the compact-range qualification. Condie’s chapter 7 offers a complementary interior excess-demand and boundary argument; the individual hypotheses for our route have been derived rather than inferred from a citation.

6. What existence leaves open

Worked case 5: multiple prices, multiple allocations and failed iteration

First let two households have u(x)=min(x₁,x₂), with endowments ((1,1),(2,2)). For a household endowed with (t,t), income is (p₁+p₂)t. At strictly positive prices, a utility level above t would require both goods above t and exceed the budget. The bundle (t,t) attains t. Any other bundle attaining at least t has both coordinates at least t, and a strict increase in either would exceed the budget. Thus demand is uniquely (t,t). Every strictly positive relative price clears both markets. Preferences are weakly monotone but fail the theorem’s strict coordinate condition: increasing a good already in excess need not help. This direct example demonstrates price multiplicity under its own assumptions.

Now use two households with u(x)=x₁+x₂ and endowment ((1,1),(1,1)). These preferences satisfy the main theorem. If p₁<p₂, every household spends only on good 1, so positive supply of good 2 cannot clear; p₁>p₂ is symmetric. A zero-priced good has no finite utility maximizer. Hence equilibrium prices must be equal. Normalize them to (1,1). Each household demands the entire segment x₁+x₂=2, x≥0. Every allocation ((a,2−a),(2−a,a)) for (0,2) as the closed interval of permissible a clears. The main theorem therefore guarantees neither a unique allocation nor a single-valued demand.

Finally, f(x)=1−x on [0,1] has the unique fixed point 1/2, but repeated application starting at zero gives (0,1,0,1,0). A continuous map may have a fixed point without its naive iteration converging. This is a mathematical counterexample to that inference, not a proposed market adjustment rule. Any stability claim about a particular economic process requires a separately specified process and proof.

Worked case 6: the preference hypothesis can decide existence

One household owns (1,1) and has u(x)=x₁²+x₂² on ℝ+2; there are no firms. Utility is continuous and strictly coordinate-increasing, including at zero. Upper contours are not convex: (2,0) and (0,2) each have utility 4, but their midpoint has utility 2.

At any positive p, wealth is p₁+p₂. Buying only the cheaper good gives quantity (p₁+p₂)/min(p₁,p₂)≥2, and hence utility at least 4, strictly more than the endowed bundle’s utility. More explicitly, on the binding budget line utility is a strictly convex quadratic in x₁, so its maximum occurs at an endpoint; the cheaper-good endpoint is a maximizing one, with both endpoints maximizing when prices tie. Market clearing with one household would require x=ω, so it is impossible at any positive price. At a zero price, free-good utility is unbounded and no optimizer exists. All nonzero nonnegative prices have been covered; there is no deterministic competitive equilibrium.

Convexifying upper contours changes preferences, while introducing lotteries changes the consumption object and its feasibility rules. A half-and-half lottery over the two endpoints can have the same mean as the endowment, but it does not deliver the endowment in each realization. Neither operation proves equilibrium for the original deterministic economy. A research claim must identify the altered economy and verify its resource constraints separately.

An excess-demand function is an additional property. The existence proof deliberately used correspondences. With strictly convex preferences, positive prices and appropriate attainment, demand may become unique and thus define a function. Even then continuity, boundary behavior or restrictions on aggregate excess demand must be established in their stated domains. Walras law and price homogeneity alone do not establish existence, uniqueness, comparative-static signs or stable adjustment.

How to read a numerical equilibrium. Verify every household’s budget, global optimality and ownership income; every firm’s original technological feasibility and global profit optimality; and all commodity balances under one consistent price normalization. A small residual only describes that candidate. It does not prove a solution exists for every admissible economy or that another equilibrium is absent. Exact derivations in cases 1 and 2 prove uniqueness there because the full branch and boundary analysis was supplied.

7. Exercises

Use exact fractions where possible. Proof questions require the stated hypotheses and the limiting or optimality argument, not a diagram alone. Cases 1–6 specify their own preferences; apply the main theorem only when all its assumptions hold.

  1. A new exchange economy. Retain case 1’s shares, but use endowments (4,3) and (1,4). Derive the demand formula from the global budget problem, find all equilibrium relative prices with p₂=1, compute incomes and allocations, and verify both budgets and both markets. Explain the exclusion of zero prices.
  2. The ownership ledger. At case 2’s equilibrium, reconstruct both incomes and allocations with shares (1/4,3/4), then with shares (1/2,1/2). Compute aggregate excess demand and its value if profits are omitted from income but the same profitable production is supplied. Explain why the ownership result does not extend automatically to households with different expenditure shares.
  3. Sperner and strict labels. Prove the parity statement in dimension d from the statement in dimension d−1, specifying all possible simplex contributions and boundary incidences. Recompute case 3’s labels and marked-edge incidence counts. Show with a concrete simplex self-map why labeling by the smallest i with vi≥fi(v), rather than a strict inequality, can violate Sperner’s boundary rule.
  4. Brouwer beyond a simplex. Prove the passage from fully labeled cells of vanishing mesh to a fixed point, explaining why nested cells are unnecessary. Prove nearest-point projection is single-valued and nonexpansive, and explain the containing-simplex extension. For K={(t,1−t):0≤t≤1}, derive the projection formula and project (2,2), (−1,0) and (2,0).
  5. Kakutani without a continuous selection. Supply the finite-net approximation proof, including the compact-range graph-to-upper-hemicontinuity implication and the final convex approximation at the limit point. Explain why arbitrary selections need not be continuous. For the constant correspondence F(x)=[1/4,3/4] on [0,1], locate every convex average of selected values; explain what this finite observation does and does not prove for general correspondences.
  6. Audit the missing hypotheses. For each of the four failures in case 4—nonconvex middle value, missing graph limit, disconnected domain and noncompact domain—identify the failed hypothesis and prove the absence of a fixed point. Prove that filling the first middle value with [0,1] restores exactly one fixed point.
  7. Build the economic correspondence. Under the theorem’s assumptions, prove the profit-income continuity and positive income bound, capped-budget approximation, demand and supply closed graphs, and convexity of their values. Define the product map including the price auction. Compute a valid resource cap for case 2 and its individual income lower bound on Δ, while explaining which part of that case does not satisfy the theorem’s preference assumptions.
  8. Clear the markets and remove the cap. Starting only from a fixed point of the product map, derive z≤0, positive prices, budget exhaustion and exact clearing in the correct order. Then prove global household optimality without assuming strict convexity. To isolate the role of convexity, use u(x)=max{0,min(x₁,x₂)−1}, x=(0,0), x′=(2,2) and λ=1/4: show that a mixture with a strictly better bundle need not be strictly better under convex preferences alone, and state which stronger theorem hypothesis this separate example lacks.
  9. Two meanings of nonuniqueness. Derive the complete positive-price equilibrium family in case 5’s Leontief economy and the complete price and allocation families in its linear economy. State which example satisfies the main theorem. Prove directly that f(x)=1−x has a unique fixed point but the iteration from zero does not converge; explain the limit on the economic conclusion.
  10. A rigorous nonexistence claim. For case 6, prove nonconvex upper contours and strictly coordinate-increasing preferences. Cover every strictly positive and boundary normalized price in the nonexistence proof. Explain why a randomized consumption proposal or a convexified preference is a different model rather than a repair of the original proof.
  11. Production branches rather than one first-order condition. Derive the firm’s supply and profit in case 2 for every w>0, including w=1/2. Exclude the capacity branch economically, solve the interior market-clearing polynomial and reject inadmissible roots. Verify that the other commodity clears and explain precisely when Walras law would be insufficient to infer that fact.
  12. Referee a claim. A paper says: “A coarse price grid returned a low residual after we convexified the production and consumption sets. Therefore every original economy has a unique equilibrium. Closed graph always means upper hemicontinuity, so arbitrary selected demands can be iterated to reach it; profits can be omitted because they are only transfers.” Write a short referee memo identifying each gap, using this chapter’s proofs or counterexamples, and specifying what evidence would support a narrower valid claim. Assess it with four equally weighted dimensions worth three points each: hypotheses and accounting; fixed-point proof and numerical scope; uniqueness and convergence; and original feasibility versus convexification.

8. Solutions and proof checkpoints

Open complete solutions

  1. A positive feasible bundle beats every axis bundle for 0<α<1, and any positive optimum spends its budget. On the binding budget, the strictly concave log objective has first-order conditions α/x₁=λr and (1−α)/x₂=λ, giving λ=1/m and demand (αm/r,(1−α)m). This proves global uniqueness of demand at each positive price. With m₁=4r+3 and m₂=r+4, aggregate first-good demand is 3+10/(3r). Setting it equal to 5 gives r=5/3, the only positive solution. Incomes are (29/3,17/3) and allocations ((58/15,29/9),(17/15,34/9)). Their expenditures are (5/3)(58/15)+29/9=29/3 and (5/3)(17/15)+34/9=17/3. They sum to (5,7), exactly the endowments. At a zero price, positive income in the priced good permits positive consumption of that good and unbounded increases of the free good, so there is no finite optimum. Every normalized boundary is thereby excluded. The uniqueness claim belongs to this economy, not to the general existence theorem.

  2. At w=1 the endowment value of either household is 2+1/2=5/2, and the firm earns 2−1=1. Adding ownership income gives (5/2+1/4,5/2+3/4)=(11/4,13/4). Equal expenditure shares divide each income equally between equally priced goods, producing ((11/8,11/8),(13/8,13/8)). With half ownership each, incomes are (3,3) and bundles ((3/2,3/2),(3/2,3/2)). Both sum to the resources (3,3). Omitting profits instead gives both incomes 5/2 and both bundles (5/4,5/4). Aggregate demand (5/2,5/2) has excess (−1/2,−1/2) and value −1. The omitted unit equals the actual profit that should have been distributed. If expenditure shares differed, changing θ would change how total profits were divided across propensities to buy each good, changing aggregate demand at given prices. The equal-share calculation provides no general invariance to ownership.

  3. Mark facets carrying exactly labels 0,…,d−1. A d-cell contributes one when all labels 0,…,d appear, two when it has exactly labels 0,…,d−1 with one repeated, and zero otherwise. Interior facets are incident twice and boundary facets once. Boundary label restrictions forbid marked facets on every original face opposite i<d; the face opposite d inherits a valid (d−1)-dimensional Sperner labeling. Its marked count is odd by induction, starting with the single point for d=0. Thus the total incidence count is odd and so is the number of fully labeled d-cells. In case 3 the deficit vectors in the table give labels (0,1,2,1,0,2); the cells have marked-facet counts (2,0,0,1). Only the central one is full. For the weak-label failure, use the constant map f(v)=e₀ and vertex v=e₂ in Δ². Then v−f(v)=(−1,0,1). The smallest nonnegative coordinate is index 1, so the weak rule labels v by 1 even though v₁=0. The strict rule would select 2 and respect the boundary. Zero sums ensure existence of a strictly positive deficit unless the vertex is already fixed; they do not justify a weak labeling rule.

  4. At level n choose a full cell with vertices vn,i carrying all labels. A compact subsequence of vn,0 converges to x; every other vn,i on that subsequence has distance at most the vanishing mesh from vn,0, so it converges to the same x. Its labeling inequality gives xi≥fi(x). Equal coordinate sums force equality for all i. No inclusion relationship among the cells is needed.

    For projection, compactness attains the nearest distance; two distinct minimizers have a midpoint whose squared distance is less by one quarter of their squared separation, contradicting minimality. For a=PK(z), differentiating feasible segments toward y∈K gives (z−a)·(y−a)≤0. Applying this twice to a=PK(z), b=PK(z′), then adding, gives ‖a−b‖²≤(z−z′)·(a−b), and Cauchy–Schwarz proves nonexpansiveness. Place K inside the simplex described in Section 3, apply simplex Brouwer to f∘PK, and observe that a fixed point lies in K because the map’s range does. Hence it is a fixed point of f.

    On the specified segment minimize (z₁−t)²+(z₂−1+t)² for 0≤t≤1. The unconstrained derivative vanishes at t=(z₁−z₂+1)/2; a strictly convex quadratic is minimized at this value clipped to [0,1]. The three projections are ((1/2,1/2),(0,1),(1,0)), respectively.

  5. If upper hemicontinuity failed at x, choose xn→x and yn∈F(xn) outside an open O containing F(x). Compact range gives a convergent subsequence of yn; closed graph puts its limit in F(x), while closedness of the complement of O puts it outside O, a contradiction. Take a finite ε/2-net and one selected yj at each site. Weights proportional to max(0,ε−distance) have a positive denominator and give a continuous convex average into K. Brouwer supplies a fixed point xε of this averaged map.

    As ε↓0, take xε→x along a subsequence. Every site with positive weight lies within ε of xε, so all such sites eventually lie in any prescribed neighborhood of x. Upper hemicontinuity puts their selected values within δ of F(x). Choose nearest points in compact F(x); convexity puts their weighted average in F(x) and the distance from xε to that average is at most δ. Since δ is arbitrary, the limit x lies in closed F(x). The proof does not presume that any selection is continuous. For example, even the constant interval correspondence admits the discontinuous selection 1/4 at rational x and 3/4 at irrational x. Every finite convex average of its selections remains in [1/4,3/4], which is enough for the averaging construction. In this special constant example, the entire fixed-point set is that interval; for a general F, an average of nearby selections need not belong to F at its own argument. The limiting and closed-graph steps remain necessary.

  6. The first graph consists of two closed segments, but {0,1} at 1/2 is nonconvex. A point below 1/2 maps to 1, a point above maps to 0, and the midpoint maps only to its two endpoints, so none is fixed. Filling its middle value with [0,1] gives nonempty compact convex values and a closed graph. Only 1/2 can be fixed by the same branch argument, and it now belongs to its image. The variant with middle value {0} has singleton convex values but omits the limit (1/2,1) of graph points (1/2−1/n,1). Its branches and midpoint again give no fixed point. The swap on {0,1} has a compact nonempty domain and is continuous, but the domain is not convex; each point maps to the other. The affine self-map on [0,1) has a convex domain and is continuous, but the domain is not compact; solving x=(1+x)/2 gives only x=1 outside it. These are separate hypothesis failures, not disproofs of Kakutani.

  7. For p≥0, disposal cannot raise value; maximizing on full Yj is equivalent in value to maximizing on compact Kj. The support difference is bounded by maxKj‖k‖ times ‖p−q‖, so πj and mi are continuous. Zero in K gives nonnegative profits, and normalized prices give mi≥minℓωiℓ>0. Each capped budget is nonempty compact convex with closed graph. For a feasible x at p and pn→p, set tn=min(1,mi(pn)/(pn·x)) when the denominator is positive, and one otherwise. Strict slack makes x eventually feasible, while binding feasibility and positive income make tn→1. Hence tnx approximates x from nearby budgets.

    Continuous utility attains its maximum. Convex upper contours make the maximizer set convex. If prices and optimizers converge, closed feasibility preserves the limit, and comparison with the just-constructed approximations of every limit-budget alternative proves it optimal. Firm maximizers have closed graph by passing the inequality pn·yn≥pn·k to the limit for each k, and convex values by linearity on convex K. The price auction has the same properties on Δ. Thus T(p,x,y)=A(z(x,y))×∏DiM(p)×∏Sj(p) meets the proved fixed-point hypotheses on Δ×CI×∏Kj.

    For case 2, aggregate endowment is (4,1), the coordinatewise generator maxima are (0,4), and resource bounds are (4,5). A valid common cap is 6. Each normalized income is at least 1/2. These technology, resource and income calculations are valid for that case. Its Cobb–Douglas preference is not strictly coordinate-monotone on the axes, so the full theorem cannot be invoked without qualification; its equilibrium was established directly.

  8. Budget feasibility and correctly distributed profits give p·z≤0. At a product fixed point p maximizes q·z over Δ, so zℓ=eℓ·z≤p·z≤0 for every ℓ. Feasibility and the resource bound then put every consumption coordinate strictly below M. A zero price would make any capped maximizer demand its entire cap in that coordinate, contradicting that bound, so p≫0. A household with budget slack could now buy a little more of a good without hitting the cap, contradicting strict monotonicity. Thus p·z=0, and positive p together with z≤0 yields z=0.

    If a preferred global affordable x′ existed, it would be nonzero. By continuity shrink it radially a little to tx′ still preferred; positive prices make it strictly cheaper than income. A small mixture with the capped optimum stays strictly below the cap and is weakly preferred by convex upper contours. It retains strict cost slack. Adding a small amount of a good makes it strictly preferred while staying in the capped budget, a contradiction. This proves uncapped optimality without replacing convexity by an unproved strict-mixture condition.

    For the proposed separate utility, upper contours for levels ≤0 are the whole orthant; for level c>0 they are {x:x₁≥1+c,x₂≥1+c}, which are convex. Yet the utilities of (0,0), (2,2) and their quarter mixture (1/2,1/2) are (0,1,0), respectively. This preference lacks strict coordinate monotonicity. It demonstrates why convexity alone warrants only weak improvement; the theorem’s final coordinate increase supplies strict improvement using an additional stated assumption.

  9. For Leontief utility and endowment (t,t), a level above t costs more than (p₁+p₂)t at any positive p, while (t,t) attains t. Since both prices are positive, any other bundle with both coordinates at least t costs strictly more. Thus demands are exactly (1,1) and (2,2), and every positive ratio clears. This statement is the complete family within the positive-price domain requested; weak monotonicity does not meet the main strict-coordinate hypothesis.

    In the linear economy unequal positive prices make both consumers buy only the cheaper good, leaving the other market uncleared. A zero price makes utility unbounded. Equal prices, normalized to (1,1), give wealth 2 and demand segments x₁+x₂=2. Clearing requires the second bundle to be the complement of the first in (2,2): ((a,2−a),(2−a,a)) with 0≤a≤2. Conversely every such allocation is feasible and optimal. The theorem applies to these continuous, convex and strictly monotone preferences, but it does not give a unique allocation. The scalar map f has fixed point x=1−x, hence x=1/2, uniquely. Its iterates from zero alternate between zero and one, so the even and odd subsequences have distinct limits. This refutes a general fixed-point-to-iteration inference; it says nothing about a specified economic adjustment process that has not been modeled.

  10. On the nonnegative orthant increasing one or more coordinates strictly increases the sum of their squares, so preferences are strictly coordinate-monotone. The upper contour through utility 4 contains (2,0) and (0,2) but excludes their midpoint (1,1), proving nonconvexity. With p≫0, single-household clearing would require x=(1,1), with utility 2. Income is p₁+p₂, and the cheaper-good endpoint purchases at least two units, giving utility at least 4. Thus the required clearing bundle is never optimal. When a normalized price has a zero coordinate, increasing that free coordinate makes utility unbounded; there is no maximizer. This covers all normalized nonnegative prices, proving nonexistence. A mean-feasible lottery over endpoints does not give feasible deterministic consumption in each outcome in this one-household economy. Changing preferences to their convexification changes the maximization problem. Either alternative needs a new model and its own feasibility and existence proof.

  11. At a positive output price normalized to one, an optimal firm uses the frontier q=2√n. Setting t=√n transforms the problem into maximizing 2t−wt² on [0,2]. Its derivative is 2−2wt and its curvature is −2w<0, so t=min(2,1/w) uniquely. For 0<w≤1/2, (n,q,π)=(4,4,4−4w), including the common boundary at w=1/2. For w>1/2, they are (1/w²,2/w,1/w). In the capacity branch all four units of leisure/input are used, but each household’s positive wealth and Cobb–Douglas preferences give positive leisure demand, so clearing is impossible.

    In the interior, total income is 4w+1+1/w; the leisure market is (4w+1+1/w)/(2w)=4−1/w². Multiplying by 2w² and rearranging gives 4w²−w−3=(w−1)(4w+3)=0. Of its roots 1 and −3/4 only 1 is positive and in the interior branch. At w=1, output consumption totals 3, equal to initial output endowment 1 plus production 2, and leisure consumption totals 3, equal to endowment 4 minus input 1. Correct profit distribution and expenditure exhaust budgets, so Walras law plus positive output price would also infer its market from leisure clearing. A zero price on the remaining good, unspent budgets or omitted profits would invalidate the respective inference. These alternatives cannot be ignored merely because one first-order condition holds.

  12. An adequate memo first requests a precise economy: original preferences and technologies, individual endowments, ownership shares and all budgets. Profit is income to its owners; removing it from budgets while retaining profitable output changes the economy and destroys the stated value identity. A compact-generator theorem can support an existence claim only after its actual continuity, convexity, monotonicity and positivity assumptions are verified. It does not cover arbitrary original technologies by renaming them.

    A low grid residual is evidence about an approximate candidate at sampled prices, not a proof for every economy. The paper needs a true existence argument or a certified error bound tied to its particular model, plus global optimality and feasibility checks. Closed graph gives upper hemicontinuity in the compact-range, closed-value setting used here; it is not an unrestricted equivalence. Kakutani does not make arbitrary selected demands continuous, and its proof supplies no convergence of their iterates. Case 5 separates existence from uniqueness and iteration, while case 6 shows how nonconvex preferences can prevent deterministic equilibrium. Convexification or lotteries must be identified as changes to primitives or feasible objects and checked in the altered model; they cannot certify original deterministic feasibility.

    Rubric, 12 points. Award 0–3 in each of four dimensions. For hypotheses/accounting, require explicit economic assumptions and correct owner income. For fixed-point/numerical scope, require the compact-range qualification and separation of finite residuals from a theorem. For uniqueness/convergence, require distinct counterarguments and a request for a specified adjustment law or a genuine uniqueness proof. For original feasibility/convexification, require recognition of the altered model and an explicit resource check. In each dimension 0 means absent or materially false, 1 identifies a concern without a valid reason, 2 gives the valid reason but an incomplete repair, and 3 gives both a justified diagnosis and a concrete repair. Equivalent defensible memos can earn full credit; no claim of empirical confirmation or universal failure is required.

9. Teach-back, retention and reproduction

Teach-back. Explain in three minutes why a fixed point of the product correspondence is not yet automatically a competitive equilibrium. State the accounting step, the cap issue and the role of positive prices.

Answer guide. The fixed point initially gives capped household optima and a price maximizer of excess demand. Correct owner income yields p·z≤0; the price maximizer then forces every component of z to be nonpositive. Feasibility bounds each consumption strictly below the chosen cap. Strict monotonicity rules out zero prices and permits budget exhaustion below that cap, after which p·z=0 forces exact clearing. Finally the cheaper-mixture-and-increase argument removes the cap, proving global household optimality. Award credit for the order and reason of every implication, not just the word “Kakutani.”

Delayed retention. Without looking back: why must the labeling inequality be strict; why is compact range needed in the closed-graph argument; which income would disappear if a profitable firm had ownership shares summing to less than one; and what does the alternating map disprove?

Answers. A strict positive deficit cannot occur in a zero coordinate and exists at every nonfixed simplex vertex. Compact range supplies a convergent subsequence of alleged escaping image values. Unassigned profit would be omitted from total household income, leaving an accounting gap equal to that undistributed profit. The alternating map disproves the assertion that naive iteration of every continuous self-map converges merely because it has a fixed point; it does not disprove Brouwer or any independently proved market stability result.

Reproduce and extend. Reconstruct the two exchange accounts, the full production branches, the six-vertex label table and the segment projections using fractions. Editorial checks recompute these quantities, finite triangulation witnesses and focused assumption interventions in standard-library Python. It is a finite verification aid; the arbitrary-dimensional proofs and universal economic statements are established by the arguments in this chapter. No external data or estimated probabilities enter these synthetic cases.

10. Sources and next questions

The source scope is deliberately limited. Mathew’s 2010 note was inspected in sections 1–2, physical pages 1–3, with equation images on pages 2–3; it supplies two-dimensional context, not our complete finite-dimensional extension. Tamuz’s notes, cover dated 2021, were inspected on pages 1, 4–7 and 13–17, with equation images on pages 14–16; the general production compactification is not imported. Condie’s author-hosted chapter 7 was read through its excess-demand propositions and boundary proof. The source record preserves retrieval versions, exact artifact bindings and these limitations. All numerical economies, transfers, counterexamples as organized here, exercises and their solutions are original instructional constructions.

The next chapter, Welfare, aggregation and social choice, asks what equilibrium can establish about efficiency and distribution, and which further assumptions make those claims valid. Existence supplies an allocation and a supporting price system under specified conditions; it supplies no social ranking by itself.

Sources and further study

  • Akhil Mathew, Sperner’s Lemma, Brouwer’s Fixed-Point Theorem, and the Subdivision of Squares into Triangles — Two-dimensional Sperner incidence parity and the deficit-label/compactness idea.
  • Omer Tamuz, General Equilibrium Theory, Lecture Notes — Preferences, profit supports, private ownership, Walras accounting and the compact price-auction architecture.
  • Scott Condie, Advanced Microeconomic Theory Class Notes, Chapter7: The Existence of General Equilibrium — Normalization, Walras law, excess demand and the need to justify price-boundary behavior.
